Action Plan:
1. Localized insect-sting reaction: commence an oral antihistamine (e.g., chlorphenamine 4 mg PO, up to 6-times/day, or a once-daily non-sedating alternative); observe for progression.  
2. Red-flag safety-netting: if any swelling of lips/tongue, stridor, worsening dyspnoea, or spreading rash occurs, attend the Emergency Department (A&E) immediately.  
3. Wound monitoring: watch the sting site for spreading erythema, heat, or pain; if these develop the patient should contact the clinic for possible antibiotic therapy.  
4. Education: written information link on anaphylaxis provided; advised on typical signs and when to seek urgent care.  
5. Anxiety management: reassurance given; advised low threshold to re-book video consult if worries recur.  
6. No routine allergy testing at this stage; consider only if reactions become recurrent.  
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: “struggling to breathe” and mild lip/tongue abnormal sensation minutes after a presumed wasp/bee sting to right arm.  
• History of presenting event  
  – Onset: immediately after sting (a few minutes before call).  
  – Current symptoms: mild subjective dyspnoea, slight right-sided lip tingling, “weird” tongue sensation, localized rash at sting site.  
  – No medications taken yet; no prior similar reactions; anxiety acknowledged by patient.  
• Past medical history: eczema; occasional anxiety/panic episodes; no previous anaphylaxis.  
• Medications: none regular; none taken today.  
• Allergies: penicillin.  
• Social history: 27-year-old male computer scientist; lives alone; owns a cat; no tobacco/alcohol history discussed.

Objective:
• General: alert, speaking full sentences; breathing appears normal on video; no audible stridor.  
• HEENT: lips/throat visualized on video – no visible swelling; oral mucosa normal.  
• Respiratory: chest movements normal; no accessory muscle use noted.  
• Skin (right arm): small puncture mark with mild erythema/blotchy rash; no visible swelling, heat, or discharge.  
• Vitals: not recorded.  
• Investigations: none performed during consult.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Insect sting – localized allergic reaction, rule out early anaphylaxis  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Localized allergic reaction to insect sting (DDx “Localized allergic reaction to insect sting – High”).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Early IgE-mediated anaphylaxis / systemic reaction (DDx – Medium): subjective dyspnoea & lip tingling but no objective findings.  
     • Anxiety/panic attack (DDx – Medium): history of anxiety; symptoms disproportionate to exam.  
   - Investigations planned: none at present; patient to self-monitor.  
   - Treatment: oral antihistamine as above; provide written anaphylaxis information.  
   - Referrals: none now; advise ED attendance if red-flag symptoms arise.

2. Sting-site infection risk (possible cellulitis)  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Observation for potential early cellulitis (DDx “Cellulitis/early skin infection – Low”).  
   - Differential diagnosis: traumatic local reaction alone.  
   - Investigations planned: none unless features of infection develop.  
   - Treatment: advise patient to seek review for possible antibiotics if redness spreads, becomes hot, or painful.  
   - Referrals: none at this stage.

3. Anxiety related to event  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Situational anxiety.  
   - Differential diagnosis: none additional.  
   - Investigations: none.  
   - Treatment: reassurance; encouraged to re-contact clinic if anxiety escalates.  
   - Referrals: none now.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: objective vitals (HR, BP, RR, SpO₂), complete medication and substance use history, vaccination status.  
● Internal conflicts: none noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; minimal background noise; all clinically relevant information intelligible.
